name: Lume whole body deodorant

lead: Lume is a deodorant brand that markets a mandelic acid formula for the whole body, aiming at fresh scent from underarms to other odor-prone areas without aluminium. It gained wide attention on short-video platforms.

As a deodorant it targets odor-causing bacteria rather than sweat; acid-based products are described as keeping skin mildly acidic. Body odor arises mainly from bacteria acting on apocrine sweat, concentrated in the armpits. Claims rest on the manufacturer and user reports, as no published study has tested it.

paras: Applied as a stick, gel or other form to clean, dry skin on underarms and other areas, as a daily routine product.
Possible skin irritation, particularly on sensitive or freshly shaved skin. It is regulated as a cosmetic in the US, and no product-specific safety trials were found.

angle.text: Lume is a viral acid-based deodorant sold for the whole body and discussed on short-video platforms as a non-aluminium option. Its popularity is clear; claims rest on the manufacturer and user reports.

lead: Lume is a deodorant brand that markets a whole-body deodorant, meant to be used beyond the underarms, built on an acid-based formula using mandelic acid. [1][2] People use it to reduce body odour in areas such as underarms, feet and skin folds, so that they smell fresher and feel more confident in close contact; for many grooming-focused users, smelling good is part of looking and presenting well. [1][3]

The product became widely discussed on short-video platforms and is a well-known example of the wider shift toward aluminium-free and acid-based deodorants. [4] As a deodorant, it is aimed at odour rather than sweat. Body odour arises mainly from bacteria breaking down secretions of the apocrine sweat glands, concentrated in the armpits. [3] In the US, deodorants are regulated as cosmetics, while antiperspirants are regulated as drugs. [4]
No published clinical trials of Lume have been located; the information below comes from the manufacturer's site and general reference works on deodorants, body odour and mandelic acid.

paras: Lume presents its product as a deodorant for the whole body, a positioning that distinguishes it from underarm-only products. [1] The central ingredient, mandelic acid, is an aromatic alpha hydroxy acid first isolated in 1831 by the German pharmacist Ferdinand Ludwig Winckler, who obtained it by heating amygdalin from bitter almonds with dilute acid; the name comes from the German word for almond, Mandel. [2]
Mandelic acid is also used in superficial chemical peels and is described as usable on all Fitzpatrick skin types. [2] Its use in a deodorant is a separate application from peeling.

sections.h: How it is described to work
paras: Sweat itself is largely odourless. Bacteria break down compounds from sweat, particularly secretions from the apocrine glands that become active at puberty, and the breakdown products produce most body odour. [3][4] Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species are among the bacteria named as contributors. [3]

Acid-based deodorants are intended to keep the skin surface mildly acidic, which is said to limit bacterial growth, in contrast to alkaline products. [4] They do not stop sweating, unlike aluminium antiperspirants, which form plugs in sweat ducts. [4]

Deodorants have a long commercial history: Mum was patented in Philadelphia in 1888, the first commercial antiperspirant appeared in 1903, and deodorant sales grew sharply in the mid-twentieth century as men became a major market. [4] Wikipedia notes that alum and other aluminium-free alternatives have become popular, and that their makers often cite concern about aluminium; it adds that scientific reviews have found little evidence linking aluminium in deodorants to cancer or Alzheimer's disease. [4]

Lume spread largely through short-video and social platforms, where it is described as a whole-body odour product. Wikipedia reports that as many as 90 percent of Americans reportedly use deodorant or antiperspirant. [3]

No Lume-specific safety studies were located. Reference sources note that deodorant ingredients can irritate skin in some users, for example propylene glycol, and that zirconium-containing antiperspirants can cause allergic reactions. [4] Acids may also irritate sensitive or freshly shaved skin. Mandelic acid is described as moderately toxic if swallowed. [2]

lore.intro: Lume spread largely through short-video platforms and social media, where it is described as a whole-body odour product. No forum material was available for this entry.

claims.claim: A deodorant can be used on the whole body, not just the underarms
